newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Saddam, Sumitomo return commodities to the headlines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Saddam, Sumitomo return commodities to the headlines.

text.p: Commodities sprang back to the headlines this month as the size of copper trading losses at Japan's Sumitomo Corp by alleged rogue trader Yasuo Hamanaka were revised up by nearly 50 percent to $2.6 billion.
This time the Sumitomo news failed to destabilise prices, in sharp contrast to early summer when copper nosedived on news of Hamanaka's unprecedented losses.

Saddam Hussein takes much of the credit for strong oil and natural gas markets as Iraqi oil supplies have again been held back from the market and consumers who had waited for lower prices have scurried to rebuild depleted stocks before the northern hemisphere winter.

But other industrial raw material and food commodity markets have generally lacked a clear trend as the traditional off-season for commodities drew to an end and dealers tried to gauge demand from industrial buyers.

Financial markets are generally more complex and commodity traders have to reckon on how attractive their markets may look to large investment funds who choose between every market from equities through bonds to foreign exchange and commodities.
Views are mixed on current fund involvement in commodities.
"Equity index markets have been the most popular game in town, but that can quickly change," bankers and analysts said.
But investment bankers and commodity brokers are acutely aware that it does not take very much in terms of total fund resources to have a major impact on a commodity price.
Earlier this year gold, copper, cocoa and grains have all had their moments.
Many analysts and bankers pin their hopes of commodity markets returning to the uptrack on increased economic growth in industrialised countries.
U.S. brokerage Merrill Lynch is hopeful for this upturn and in a recent analysis of market cycles concluded that higher commodity prices would result from accelerating economic growth.

"A resurgence in global activity in 1997 should see higher commodity prices," said Merrill analysts Trevor Greetham and Bijal Shahin a report on the survey noting commodities were strong in 1994, 1987 and 1983, when global activity accelerated.
The Merrill analysts recommend "some bottom fishing" as they expect commodities and related stocks to outperform if global activity accelerates in the wake of a spurt in money supply.
But this broad brush picture of commodity prices tending to rise when the world economy is buoyant does not remove the difficulty of choosing the winners, traders said.
This year has seen big swings in some of the markets most favoured by major hedge funds. But for varying reasons most of these have retreated from first half year highs.
Specialist analysts and investment bankers agree windows of opportunity do or will exist in several markets but many are reluctant to point to a single one as offering the best chance.
Some admit to being put off making too strong predictions by the sharpness of some of the price reversals this year.
Extra output or reduced stocks boosted supplies in some markets which were "hot" early this year and prices retreated.
Much more is now known of supply and demand in the former Soviet Union but China remains the big "an unknown" for many commodities.
This is particularly true for copper where it could be the trigger to turn prices higher after the mid-year battering.
But analysts agree that new mines now being developed should place the red metal firmly in surplus by mid-1997.

Senior traders say it takes time to establish a new meaningful level after such a huge speculative position as Sumitomo's has had to be absorbed. Huge premiums paid for immediate delivery in June have disappeared, but could soon return if a recent pick-up in demand continues.
This new tightening in supplies worsened when scrap supplies -- an important source of supplies --dried up after the Sumitomo linked price collapse.

Now record high grain crops are being reported and prices for wheat and corn are well below the peaks although a debate still rages on whether the world is bumping against natural limits on its ability to feed an ever growing population or whether it can increase yields and planted acreage.
There is little room for complacency but some analysts said the untangling of rigid farm support prices encourages farmers to respond more quickly to price moves.

This is likely to lead to more volatile markets and already London is researching new futures contracts that will give farmers across Europe a vital forward market to protect themselves from the expected more volatile grain prices.
Cocoa has long been a favourite of speculators thanks to conflicting news on crops deep in tropical areas of West Africa, Brazil or Asia.

Added to this uncertain background this year has seen an apparent shift in ownership of surplus stocks to a single trader and a feared return to a deficit in world production which could make these stocks a valuable commodity.
